why_how.text: A smooth start and a controlled stop are the foundation of every drive.
The checks before moving and before stopping prevent the most basic collisions.

scenario.text: Nia gets into a borrowed car, starts it and wants to pull out of a driveway.

reasoning.text: She keeps her right foot on the brake with the gear in park to start, then shifts to drive, checks all around and signals.

result.text: Nia presses the accelerator gently and builds speed slowly and evenly with her heel on the floor.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a stop starts by pressing the brake.

correction.text: Stopping begins with a mirror check for traffic behind, and only then does your foot move to the brake.

memory_support.text: Brake, park, key to start; mirrors, then brake to stop.

prompt.text: Which gear should the selector be in as you start the engine?

rationale.text: You start in park and move to drive only when you are ready to pull away.

narration.text: Every drive begins and ends the same way: you start the engine, pull away safely and come to a controlled stop. Each of those steps has its own order and its own checks. In this unit you will learn how to start the engine correctly, what to look at once it is running, how to pull away, how to build speed smoothly and how to stop. Because vehicles differ, your owner's manual is the place to learn how to start the particular vehicle you are driving. Each of these steps takes only seconds once it becomes a habit. Following the same order every time makes the routine automatic.

lines.text: Key on or push the button

narration.text: To start the engine, put your right foot on the brake pedal, confirm the gear selector is in park, then turn the key to the on position or push and release the start button. Once the engine runs, look over the gauges and any dashboard indicator lights that need attention, such as fuel, oil, ABS or air bag warnings. A warning light at start-up is the vehicle telling you something, so deal with it before you drive rather than after you are on the road. A calm, unhurried start sets the tone for the whole drive. These habits matter just as much on short trips as on long ones.

To pull away, move the gear selector to D for drive and make sure the path ahead of the vehicle is safe. Before moving, also check the sides, the rear and your blind spots, looking over your shoulder for any traffic or obstacles. Then give a signal and, if it is safe, move your foot to the accelerator and press it gently. Build speed slowly and evenly, pressing the pedal with the top of your foot while your heel rests on the floor. Smooth control also makes the ride more comfortable for passengers. Practice the routine until you no longer have to think about it.

Here is a simple trap. The gear selector should be in park when you start the engine, and you move it to D for drive only when you are ready to pull away. Starting in drive, or shifting before you have checked around the vehicle, removes the moment that lets you look for traffic and obstacles. Keep the order: brake, park and start; then check the gauges; then shift to drive, check all around, signal and accelerate gently. Each step gives you a chance to catch a problem. Drivers behind you appreciate smooth, predictable stops. A careful start avoids many low-speed mistakes.

To stop, first check your mirrors for traffic behind you, then shift your foot from the accelerator to the brake pedal. Keep steady pressure on the brake pedal until the vehicle has stopped. Checking the mirrors first tells you whether someone is close behind, which helps you decide how gently to slow. Stopping begins with that mirror check, and only then does your foot move to the brake. Smooth, steady pressure is easier on passengers and gives drivers behind you time to react. Smooth stops also protect your passengers and the vehicle itself.

Here is a quick check: you sit down in the driver's seat and get ready to start the engine. Which gear should the selector be in? The answer is park. You put your right foot on the brake, confirm the selector is in park, then turn the key or push the start button. You move it to D for drive only when you are ready to pull away, after checking the gauges and looking ahead, to the sides, behind and over your shoulder. With that order in place, every start-up becomes routine. Check the gauges once the engine runs, and then you are ready to pull away safely.

To close, check the owner's manual for how to start your vehicle. Start with your right foot on the brake and the gear in park, then check the gauges and warning lights. To pull away, shift to drive, make sure the path ahead is safe, check the sides, rear and blind spots, signal and accelerate gently, building speed slowly and evenly with your heel down. To stop, check your mirrors first, then move to the brake and keep steady pressure until the vehicle stops. These basics come before every other skill in this manual.

why_how.text: A good grip and the right hand positions give you control and protect you in a crash.
Push-pull steering is the method for most of your driving.

scenario.text: Eli holds the wheel at ten and two with his thumbs hooked inside the rim, as an older relative taught him.

reasoning.text: The manual places the hands at seven to nine and three to five, with fingers on the outside and thumbs up along the face.

result.text: Eli lowers his hands to those areas and uses push-pull steering, so his arms never cross the wheel.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking hands at ten and two are still the safest position.

correction.text: The two and ten position is not recommended because it can be dangerous in vehicles with air bags.

memory_support.text: Hands low, fingers out, thumbs up; push up, slide, pull down.

prompt.text: Picturing the wheel as a clock, where does your left hand belong for normal driving?

answer.text: In the seven to nine o'clock area.

rationale.text: The left hand belongs at seven to nine and the right at three to five.

narration.text: How you hold the steering wheel affects your control, your comfort and your safety in a crash. In this unit you will learn which way to turn the wheel, how to grip it, where your hands belong on the clock face, when a hand may leave the wheel, and how push-pull steering works. You will also learn where to practice as a beginner and when you are ready for turning and parking. These basics shape every turn you make, so they are worth learning precisely. Good habits with your hands make every turn smoother. These positions may feel unfamiliar at first, but they soon become natural.

lines.text: Turn toward where you want to go
Fingers, thumbs up, outside the rim

narration.text: You turn the steering wheel toward the direction you want the vehicle to go, whether you are moving forward or in reverse. Hold the outside of the wheel with both hands on opposite sides, using a grip that is firm but gentle. Grip with your fingers rather than your palms, keep your thumbs up along the face of the wheel, and never turn it while holding the inside of the rim. Hooked thumbs or a hand inside the rim can be injured if the wheel spins suddenly. Practice the grip in a parked vehicle until it feels comfortable. A relaxed but firm grip helps you feel the road.

Picturing the wheel as a clock face, your left hand belongs in the seven to nine o'clock area and your right hand in the three to five o'clock area. Both hands stay on the wheel at all times except when one is needed for another driving task, such as shifting gears, switching on the wipers or giving hand signals. The hand signals that may take one hand off the wheel are those for turning, slowing or stopping. Once the task is done, the hand goes straight back. Lower hands also leave room for the air bag to work as designed. Small corrections are part of every stretch of straight road.

lines.text: Used above ten to fifteen miles per hour
Start at seven to eight and four to five

narration.text: Hand-to-hand steering, usually called push-pull steering, is the method for turning the wheel in normal forward driving above ten to fifteen miles per hour. Your left hand holds the wheel between seven and eight o'clock and your right between four and five. One hand pushes the wheel up while the other slides up, grips and pulls down, and the pushing hand slides back toward its start to make adjustments. To return to your intended path, simply reverse the hand motions. Push-pull steering keeps your movements compact and controlled.

Here is the trap. Many drivers learned to hold the wheel at ten and two, and they still believe it is the safest grip. The manual says otherwise: push-pull is the preferred steering method, and the two and ten o'clock position is not recommended because it can be dangerous in vehicles with air bags. Keep your hands lower, in the seven to nine and three to five areas, so a deploying air bag does not drive your hands and arms toward your face. Breaking an old habit takes practice, so rehearse the lower grip until it feels normal. Your hands will thank you on long drives, and your face is better protected if the air bag deploys.

lines.text: Safer with a driver's air bag

narration.text: Keeping your hands in the seven to nine and three to five areas tends to reduce muscle strain, which means less steering that causes weaving within a lane. In push-pull steering your arms stay next to your body, which makes it more natural to keep both hands on the wheel the whole time. And since your hands and arms never cross over the wheel, a frontal crash in a vehicle with a driver's air bag is less likely to injure your face, hands and arms. Lower hands and compact movements give you the best control. Together, these benefits make push-pull the preferred method.

lines.text: Where does the left hand go?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: picture the steering wheel as a clock face. Where does your left hand belong during normal driving? The answer is in the seven to nine o'clock area, with your right hand in the three to five o'clock area. For push-pull steering, the hands start a little lower still, at seven to eight and four to five. Avoid the two and ten position, which is not recommended in vehicles with air bags, and keep both hands on the wheel except for driving tasks. Practicing the hand positions until they feel natural pays off on every drive. Keep both hands in those areas whenever you are not doing another driving task.

lines.text: Grip outside, fingers and thumbs up
Hands at seven to nine and three to five

narration.text: To close, turn the wheel toward where you want to go, forward or in reverse, holding the outside of the rim with both hands, fingers gripping and thumbs up. Keep your left hand at seven to nine and your right at three to five, and take a hand off only for driving tasks such as shifting, wipers or turning, slowing and stopping signals. Use push-pull steering above ten to fifteen miles per hour, avoid the two and ten grip, and practice first on lightly traveled rural roads until your steering is accurate enough for turning and parking.

why_how.text: Different situations call for different steering methods, so choosing well keeps you in control.
Keeping one hand on the wheel during any reach protects balance and safety.

scenario.text: Zoe is pulling into a tight parking space at very low speed.

reasoning.text: Hand-over-hand steering is used at low speeds, such as at intersections or while parking.

result.text: Zoe starts with her hands at eight to nine and three to four and uses the top third of the wheel to turn.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking one-hand steering is fine for relaxed highway driving.

correction.text: One-hand steering is only for backing up or a short reach to controls such as the wipers, flashers or lights.

memory_support.text: Push-pull for normal speeds, hand-over-hand for slow turns, one hand only for backing or a quick reach.

prompt.text: During a reach for the wipers, what hand position does the hand left on the wheel keep?

answer.text: The normal operating position of eight to nine or three to four o'clock.

rationale.text: The hand that stays keeps the normal position, which matches where hand-over-hand starts.

narration.text: Push-pull steering covers most of your driving, but it is not the only method. Hand-over-hand steering handles slow, sharp turns, and one-hand steering is allowed in only two narrow situations. In this unit you will learn when each method fits, where your hands start for hand-over-hand steering, how it works, and why one hand must always stay on the wheel even when the other is busy. Choosing the right method for each moment keeps the vehicle balanced and under your control. Practice each method in an empty parking lot before using it in traffic.

lines.text: Start at eight to nine and three to four
Top third of the wheel leads

narration.text: Hand-over-hand steering is for turning the wheel at low speeds, for example at an intersection or while parking. Start with your left hand between eight and nine o'clock and your right hand between three and four o'clock. Use the right top third of the wheel to turn right and the left top third to turn left, repeating the motion as needed. Then reverse the process to straighten out. The method lets you turn the wheel far and quickly when the vehicle is barely moving. The right method makes a tight turn feel easy and controlled. Switching methods smoothly is a skill that improves with practice.

Here is the trap: using the wrong method for the situation. Hand-over-hand steering is for low-speed turns such as at intersections or when parking, while push-pull is the preferred method for normal driving. Push-pull keeps your arms from crossing the wheel, which matters when an air bag might deploy at speed. Hand-over-hand crosses your hands, which is fine at a crawl but not ideal at highway speeds. Let the speed and the situation decide which method you use. Every method keeps at least one hand on the wheel. Low speeds give you time to use hand-over-hand carefully.

lines.text: Only for backing or a short reach

narration.text: One-hand steering is only for backing up or for a short reach to controls such as the wipers, flashers or lights. When you must reach for a control, keep your other hand at the normal operating position of eight to nine or three to four o'clock, depending on how the wheel is designed. That hand keeps the same areas where hand-over-hand steering starts. Make the reach quick, return the hand to the wheel, and save any longer adjustments for when the vehicle is stopped. Keep reaches short and save longer adjustments for a stop. Balance and control come from good hand placement.

Keeping one hand on the wheel at all times matters for vehicle balance, for handling steering reversals and for avoiding injury. If both hands leave the wheel, even briefly, a bump or a sudden need to correct can catch you with no control at all. The hand that stays in its normal position can make small corrections and is ready for more steering if needed. This is why the manual limits one-hand steering to backing and short reaches rather than relaxed cruising. That is why the manual keeps one-hand steering for brief, specific moments.

Here is a quick check: you reach over to switch on the wipers while driving. Where should your other hand be? The answer is at the normal operating position of eight to nine or three to four o'clock, depending on the wheel design. Those are the same areas where hand-over-hand steering starts. Keeping that hand in place protects vehicle balance, lets you handle steering reversals and helps you avoid injury. Make the reach quick, then return both hands to the wheel. A quick reach and a quick return keep the vehicle steady.

lines.text: One hand only for backing or a reach

narration.text: To close, push-pull is the preferred steering method, and the two and ten position is not recommended in vehicles with air bags. Hand-over-hand steering is for low-speed turns such as intersections and parking, starting at eight to nine and three to four and using the top third of the wheel. One-hand steering is only for backing up or a short reach to controls, and the other hand stays at the normal operating position to keep the vehicle balanced and to help you avoid injury. Choosing the right method for each moment keeps you in control at every speed.

why_how.text: Backing is slow but risky, because the area right behind the vehicle is hard to see.
A set routine for backing keeps you in control in a direction that is harder to steer.

scenario.text: Max needs to back out of a driveway where neighborhood children often play.

reasoning.text: Children and small objects cannot be seen from the driver's seat, so you check behind the vehicle before getting in.

result.text: Max walks behind the car, then gets in, holds the wheel at twelve with his left hand and backs out slowly while looking through the rear window.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking the mirrors or camera show everything behind you.

correction.text: Mirrors do not show the area right behind the vehicle, so your main view comes from looking through the rear window.

memory_support.text: Walk around, brake, reverse, left hand at twelve, look back, go slow.

prompt.text: What makes children and small objects behind a vehicle easy to miss when backing?

answer.text: Because children and small objects cannot be seen from the driver's seat.

rationale.text: The area right behind the vehicle is hidden from the driver, so a walk-around comes first.

narration.text: Backing up happens at low speed, but it carries its own risks. The area right behind your vehicle is hard to see, and a vehicle is much harder to steer in reverse. In this unit you will learn the backing routine from start to finish: checking behind before you get in, setting your hands and body, where to look, how to use mirrors and cameras, how fast to go, how to steer and how long to keep looking back. Following the same routine every time keeps people and property behind you safe. Backing slowly gives everyone around you time to react.

Check behind the vehicle before you get in, because children and small objects cannot be seen from the driver's seat. That walk-around takes only seconds, and it is the one step that lets you see the space your mirrors and windows miss. Then, to back up, keep your foot on the brake, shift into reverse and take hold of the wheel at twelve o'clock with your left hand. Do not shift into reverse until you have checked behind, especially where children may be playing. A careful routine protects children, pets and property behind you. Practice backing in an empty lot before trying it in tight spaces.

lines.text: Only when backing left or right

narration.text: A twelve o'clock hand position is recommended only when you back up to the left or right and must turn in your seat to see the path behind you. Backing up is the only situation in which the manual recommends the twelve o'clock position, and its backing steps put your left hand there. That position lets you turn your upper body toward the rear while still steering with one hand. In normal forward driving, your hands return to the lower positions of the clock face. Most backing mistakes come from moving too fast or looking in the wrong place.

lines.text: Right arm on the passenger seat
Mirrors and camera now and then

narration.text: Rest your right arm on the back of the passenger seat and look straight out through the rear window. Glance at your mirrors from time to time while backing, knowing they do not show the area right behind the vehicle, and check a rearview camera now and then if you have one. When reversing, your main view comes from turning to look through the rear window, while the mirrors and camera are only occasional checks. The rear window gives you the widest, most direct view of your path. Take your time; there is no prize for backing quickly. Each step in the routine covers a different blind area.

lines.text: Look back as your main view

narration.text: Here is the trap. Many drivers back up using only the mirrors or a camera, assuming they show everything. They do not. Mirrors do not show the area right behind the vehicle, and the manual treats mirrors and a camera as things to check now and then, not as your main view. Your main view comes from turning in your seat and looking through the rear window. Combine that with the walk-around before you get in, and you cover the hidden area as well as possible. Patience is the most important tool when backing up. Keep your foot ready to brake throughout the maneuver.

lines.text: Steer toward where the rear goes
Check front and sides when turning

narration.text: Accelerate gently and keep your speed low in reverse, because a vehicle is much harder to steer when backing. While backing, steer a little toward the side you want the rear of the vehicle to move. If you are turning while you back up, make quick checks to the front and both sides, because the front of the vehicle swings out as you turn. Small, slow steering movements give you time to correct, while fast backing can turn a small mistake into a collision. If the vehicle starts moving faster than you can steer comfortably, brake and start again more slowly.

lines.text: Before getting in to back up

narration.text: Here is a quick check: before getting into a vehicle to back out of a driveway, why should you walk around and check behind it? The answer is that children and small objects cannot be seen from the driver's seat. Your mirrors do not show the area right behind the vehicle either. So the walk-around comes first, then the backing routine: foot on the brake, shift to reverse, left hand at twelve o'clock, right arm on the passenger seat and your eyes looking through the rear window. That routine, repeated every time, is the safest way to back up.

lines.text: Look back, go slow, steer slightly

narration.text: To close, check behind the vehicle before you get in, because children and small objects cannot be seen from the driver's seat. Keep your foot on the brake, shift to reverse and hold the wheel at twelve o'clock with your left hand, the one situation where twelve is recommended. Rest your right arm on the passenger seat, look through the rear window, and check mirrors and any camera now and then. Go slowly, steer slightly toward where the rear should go, check the front and sides when turning, and keep looking back until you stop.
